title: The balance
hook: He set the balance, so don't transgress it: weigh justly (55:7–9)

segments.voice: Yesterday: bayan, clear speech, a gift from the Merciful, and your line, taught to speak.

At a market stall, a woman scoops lentils onto an old brass scale. The pan dips; she adds a pinch, takes a pinch away, and waits until the needle sits dead center. The customer watches the needle, not her face. Both know how easy it would be to lean a thumb on the pan. Surah Ar-Rahman, a few verses after speech, lifts its eyes to the whole sky. Then, in the same breath, it comes straight back down to that scale.
screen: `A BRASS SCALE AT A MARKET STALL.`

segments.voice: Verses seven to nine. Pickthall: "And the sky He hath uplifted; and He hath set the measure, That ye exceed not the measure, But observe the measure strictly, nor fall short thereof." Pickthall says measure; the Arabic is mizan, three times in three short verses. Mizan comes from the root w-z-n, to weigh: a balance, a pair of scales. Look at what sits side by side: a sky raised high, and a balance set down. Commentators read the first mizan as the order God built into creation, everything in proportion. Then the next two verses turn it into a command for people. Don't transgress in the balance. Set up the weight with justice, and don't make the balance short. The cosmic order and the shopkeeper's scale are the same word. Cheating at a scale isn't small in this picture; it's a crack in the order that holds up the sky. The Qur'an returns to this elsewhere. Surah Al-Mutaffifin opens with woe to those who take full measure for themselves and give short measure to others. The prophet Shu'ayb told his people again and again to give full measure and weight. And the Mizan has one more meaning. On the Day of Judgment, the Qur'an says, God will set up just scales, and no soul will be wronged in the least. So the word stretches from the stars, to the market, to the last day: one balance, kept fair at every size.
screen: `MIZAN: FROM W-Z-N, TO WEIGH.` · `THE SKY RAISED, THE BALANCE SET.` · `DON'T MAKE THE BALANCE SHORT.` · `JUST SCALES ON THE LAST DAY.`

segments.voice: Let your breath even out, in and out the same length, like two pans settling. Then think of one place where a scale tips your way a little, work you claim, time you take, praise you hand out unevenly, and picture setting the needle back to center.
Mizan. The balance, from the root to weigh: the order of creation, the honest scale, and the just scales of the last day. Today's word.
Your line: keep the balance. One word spans the sky and the market scale. That's day six hundred four.

howItsDone: Islamic law has long treated honest weights and measures as a religious duty; historically a market inspector, the muhtasib, checked traders' scales, and these verses of Ar-Rahman are quoted as a reminder of fair dealing.

what a scholar hears: mizan, from w-z-n, three times in 55:7–9; commentators link it to justice ('adl), and the plural mawazin names the scales of the Day of Judgment (21:47).

chat.says: Why would a surah about the sky talk about weighing groceries?
options: Mizan names both creation's order and an honest scale; cheating cracks both.
It's only a figure of speech; the Qur'an doesn't care much about trade.
Because merchants in Mecca weighed their goods for the Ka'bah.
chat.meaning: 55:7–9 uses mizan three times: the balance set in creation, and the command not to transgress it or make it short.
